references.text: In the immediate context, Jesus speaks about how the day of the Son of Man will come suddenly, just as in the days of Noah and Lot—people were eating, drinking, and living normally, but were suddenly struck by judgment. Verse 34 illustrates this suddenness: two are lying in the same bed, but only one is taken ([ref:Luk 17:26-30|Luke 17:26-30]).

Matthew's parallel passage describes the same thing: "Then two men will be out in the field; one is taken, one is left. Two women will be grinding at the mill; one is taken, one is left." This is the clearest parallel to Luke 17:34 ([ref:Matt 24:40-41|Matthew 24:40-41]).

Jesus emphasizes that no one knows when the Lord will come, and therefore one must stay awake—the sudden separation between those who are taken and those who are left requires vigilance ([ref:Matt 24:42-44|Matthew 24:42-44]).

Paul describes the coming of the Lord, where believers will be caught up to meet the Lord, which can be seen in connection with "one is taken" while the other is left behind ([ref:1 Tess 4:16-17|1 Thessalonians 4:16-17]).

The day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night—this connects to the nighttime motif in Luke 17:34 ("that night") and the unexpected nature of the separation ([ref:1 Tess 5:2-3|1 Thessalonians 5:2-3]).

Jesus' parable about the thief who comes unexpectedly at night points to the same theme: the Son of Man will come at an hour when you do not expect it, and you must be ready ([ref:Luk 12:39-40|Luke 12:39-40]).

During the flood, all life was wiped out while only Noah and those with him in the ark were spared. This illustrates the sudden separation between those who are saved and those left behind in judgment, as Jesus refers to in the context ([ref:1 Mos 7:21-23|Genesis 7:21-23]).

Lot was led out of Sodom while the others were left for judgment. Jesus uses the time of Lot as an example in the context (Luke 17:28-29), and the sudden separation in verse 34 reflects this ([ref:1 Mos 19:15-17|Genesis 19:15-17]).
